question.q: Describe the Cru Bourgeois du Médoc classification as it has worked since its 2020 relaunch.
accept: three tiers of cru bourgeois revalidated every five years
cru bourgeois superieur and exceptionnel awarded on a five year cycle
tiered classification with an audit and a five year expiry
three levels that expire and must be re-earned
question.ans: Three tiers — Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel — awarded to the château on blind tasting plus an audit of production, traceability and environmental practice, and revalidated on a five-year cycle instead of held for life
question.exp: The history explains the design. The 2003 classification was annulled by the French courts in 2007 as procedurally unfair to the excluded; from 2010 to 2018 the name survived only as an annual selection of individual wines, not of estates. The 2020 return to a classification of estates works precisely because it expires — a ranking that must be re-earned is far harder to sue over than one held in perpetuity. Contrast 1855, which has never expired and has been altered once.

findings.claim: Metallic clash risk comes from tannin and oak, not white wine per se.
findings.because: Tamura et al. (J. Agric. Food Chem. 2009) showed that the fishy-metallic aftertaste in wine and seafood pairings is driven by ferrous iron in the wine, not by tannin: adding Fe2+ to model wine raised it, chelating iron in red wine suppressed it, and intensity tracked total iron and ferrous ion. The bank's own explanation for a-9x83xbqa already says the aftertaste "tracks the wine's iron", so the two explanations contradict each other.
findings.fix: The fishy-metallic clash tracks the wine's iron content (Tamura 2009), not tannin, oak or white wine as such; low-iron, unoaked, high-acid whites are the safe choice.
findings.verifyReason: The finding holds. Question a-1sstd67g's model answer is fine (Muscadet, Chablis, Fino and brut nature with oysters). Its explanation says "Metallic clash risk comes from tannin and oak, not white wine per se". That is the traditional belief, and Tamura et al. (J. Agric. Food Chem. 2009, 57(18):8550-8556) disproved it. Across the red and white wines they tasted with scallops, the fishy aftertaste tracked total iron and ferrous iron. Adding Fe2+ to model wine made it stronger, and binding the iron in red wine suppressed it. Ferrous iron speeds up the oxidation of the seafood's unsaturated fats into aldehydes such as hexanal, heptanal and 1-octen-3-one. The authors conclude that even tannic reds can suit seafood when their iron is low, so "tannin and oak" is the wrong cause. The same batch also contradicts itself: the explanation for a-9x83xbqa already says the aftertaste "tracks the wine's iron". The examiner's fix is right in substance but slightly off. It lists oak as something the paper ruled out (the paper never tested oak), and it treats "unoaked" as part of avoiding the metallic clash, when unoaked is really a matter of style. The better fix names iron as the cause and keeps the oyster-matching logic separate. I could not open the ACS page (403) or PubMed (CAPTCHA). The abstract's findings were confirmed through the ScienceDaily/ACS press release and the abstract quoted in search results.
findings.finalFix: High acid and a saline, mineral echo match the oyster's brine, and no oak with modest alcohol keeps the wine from swamping its delicacy. The fishy-metallic clash tracks the wine's iron (Tamura 2009), not tannin, oak or colour as such.

findings.verifyReason:
The examiner is right: the accept entry grades a wrong answer as correct.

**The law.** The Marsala DOC disciplinare sets these ageing categories:
- Fine: at least 1 year
- Superiore: at least 2 years
- Superiore Riserva: at least 4 years
- Vergine e/o Soleras: at least 5 years
- Vergine e/o Soleras Stravecchio or Riserva: at least 10 years

So the two top tiers are Vergine/Soleras and Vergine Stravecchio/Riserva, which is what the model answer says. Superiore Riserva is a separate category below both.

**The grader.** In `matchSA` (`C:/Users/zpull/SommeliersCodex/js/core.js`), the entry "superiore riserva vergine soleras" matches as a whole phrase. Its "core" rule also accepts any run of 3 or more whole words taken from it. That means "Superiore Riserva and Vergine/Soleras" is marked correct, and so is "superiore riserva vergine". Both name Superiore Riserva as a peak tier, which is false.

**The fix.** Replacing the entry with "vergine soleras and vergine stravecchio riserva" works. Because it is 6 words long, the core rule's 4-word minimum stops short fragments like "vergine and" from being accepted. Correct answers such as "Vergine/Soleras and Vergine Stravecchio/Riserva" still grade.
findings.finalFix: vergine soleras and vergine stravecchio riserva
